tier_reason: Well-known independent third-party suite (szilard/benchm-ml, 1.9k stars) with public scripts (3-boosting/1-gbm.R, 2-boost.py, 6-xgboost.R) and install/version notes (0-init/1-install.md, 0-init/1a-versions.txt) showing XGBoost training faster than R gbm and scikit-learn GradientBoostingClassifier; not A because no CPU model (only EC2 c3.8xlarge/r3.8xlarge) and no compiler or flags are stated (xgboost was built from source by devtools::install_github with R's default flags).

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Per 0-init/1-install.md, xgboost's R-package was built from GitHub source with devtools::install_github on Ubuntu 14.04 (R's default compiler flags); scikit-learn came from Anaconda 2.2.0 and gbm from CRAN.
corrections.caveats: Independent third-party suite (szilard/benchm-ml, scripts 3-boosting/1-gbm.R, 2-boost.py, 6-xgboost.R) but the comparison is not like for like. Threads: xgboost used nthread = detectCores() (32 cores) while the README calls R gbm 'a single-threaded implementation', and scikit-learn's GradientBoostingClassifier is also single-threaded, so most of the 5-9x gap over R gbm is core count. Encoding: the scikit-learn script one-hot encodes the categoricals into a dense pandas frame (pd.get_dummies), and the README itself says 'Python is very slow with one-hot encoding of categoricals, but almost as fast as R (just 1.5x slower) with simple/integer encoding', so the 183x and 375x ratios against scikit-learn mostly measure that dense encoding, not the boosting code; xgboost received a sparse.model.matrix. Hyperparameters are matched only approximately and the resulting models differ somewhat in AUC. Versions date from 2015 (xgboost 0.4-0 GitHub snapshot 2015-05-16, scikit-learn 0.15.2 before HistGradientBoostingClassifier existed, R 3.2.0); the benchmark's own May 2017 update says LightGBM is now the fastest GBM tool and moved GBM tracking to szilard/GBM-perf; scikit-learn only ran for 10K and 100K rows and R gbm has no 10M run in experiment A. CPU model and compiler flags are not stated (EC2 c3.8xlarge, r3.8xlarge occasionally for larger runs). XGBoost is itself an incumbent of this category and the comparison is off the category's listed baselines (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor). The KDD 2016 paper (arXiv 1603.02754) could not be opened (arxiv.org, ar5iv and mirrors EGRESS_BLOCKED); a search snippet says its Higgs-1M exact-greedy comparison (dense data so scikit-learn could run) has XGBoost 'more than 10x faster than scikit-learn' and R gbm faster per tree only because it expands one branch with lower accuracy (snippet only, numbers not recorded). The repo's demo/kaggle-higgs/speedtest.py publishes no numbers.

notes: All claimed numbers match the Boosting table in the benchm-ml README (e.g. 1M A 400 vs 3000 s R, 10K A 6 vs 1100 s Python; derived ratios are correct). Main shortcomings: 32 threads vs single-threaded baselines, scikit-learn timed on dense one-hot input that the README itself says makes it slow (1.5x of R with integer encoding), 2015 versions, and an off-category baseline.

tier_reason: First-party README table against FAISS on unspecified Intel Sapphire Rapids hardware with no compiler, flags, thread count or published harness for the headline indexing table (the linked unum.cloud blog is EGRESS_BLOCKED); the newer first-party RetriEval suite has public code but states only 'dual socket Intel Xeon6' and no compiler or flags, so it is not A either.

corrections.caveats: First-party README numbers only: the linked benchmark blog (unum.cloud, 2023-11-07) was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the setup behind the indexing-time table could not be checked, and the README gives no exact CPU model, thread count, compiler or flags (hence tier C). The 10x headline holds only for 96d vectors; 1536d gains are 2.3-4.4x. Default HNSW hyper-parameters differ between the libraries (BENCHMARKS.md: FAISS M=32, efConstruction 40, ef 16; USearch M=16, 128, 64), and the README asserts but does not show 'equivalent recall'. The author's newer reproducible suite (ashvardanian/RetriEval, which BENCHMARKS.md now points to; USearch v2.25 vs FAISS v1.12.0 static via faiss-sys 0.7.0, dual-socket Intel Xeon 6 with 192 threads, compiler and flags not stated) does not reproduce 10x at equal settings: SIFT 10M u8 (M=16, ef 128/256, recall@10 0.9938 vs 0.9952) gives 35,405 vs 26,374 adds/s (1.34x) and 80,729 vs 38,278 searches/s (2.11x); Turing-ANNS 10M f32 (M=48) gives 8,532 vs 7,491 adds/s (1.14x) while FAISS searches faster, 16,486 vs 12,331/s (1.34x in FAISS's favour); with bf16/f16 storage USearch leads 2.76-4.31x on adds and 1.63-2.02x on search; on PubChem MACCS binary 10M FAISS (M=64, ef 40/16, a different config) is faster, 95,230 vs 36,347 adds/s and 293,795 vs 35,767 searches/s at similar recall, but FAISS was killed at 9 h at 100M on MACCS and SIFT while USearch finished in 54.6 and 48.7 min (all ratios derived from page data). The 55.3 ms vs 2.54 ms exact-search figures come from comment 1666650778 on issue #176 that the README links; the comment did not render here, and the issue's own original report (500 vectors x 1024d, k=50, Colab) measured USearch at 94.7 ms vs FAISS IndexFlatL2 at 1.14 ms (issue labelled bug, invalid, released), so the exact-search result is workload- and version-dependent. In-tree BENCHMARKS.md has USearch-only QPS tables (Graviton 3, c7g.metal) with no FAISS rows; python/scripts/bench_exact.py can run '--backend usearch,faiss' for reproduction. Category kept as autodiff-and-ml-kernels (FAISS sits there in the catalog); it is a vector-search/ANN library, off the category's listed baselines.

notes: README numbers are quoted correctly (indexing table and 55.3 vs 2.54 ms). Main shortcomings: unverifiable first-party headline (blog blocked, no CPU model or flags), unequal default HNSW parameters, and the author's own newer RetriEval suite shows only 1.1-1.3x faster f32 builds at equal settings, FAISS faster f32 search on Turing-ANNS and much faster on binary MACCS at 10M.

tier_reason: The only number reachable is a one-line '3x faster than Base log' claim with a five-line @elapsed snippet in the Julia binding's README (no hardware, versions or methodology); the mirror's examples/c/sources/Entropy.c times libm log against yepMath_Log at -O3 but publishes no results, and the project's own MKL/libm comparisons and PPAM 2013 paper were unreachable.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 39 stars on the unofficial GitHub mirror wdv4758h/Yeppp (7 forks); the Julia binding JuliaMath/Yeppp.jl has 54 stars (archived 2020-04-09)
corrections.caveats: The only number reachable is a one-line claim in the Yeppp.jl (Julia binding) README ('Yeppp's vectorized log is 3x faster than the one in Base, which is written in Julia') with a five-line @elapsed example: one cold run each, no warm-up, no hardware, Julia version, compiler or flags. The baseline is Julia's own scalar log, not <cmath>/libm, the baseline of the math-simd-linear-algebra category this record is now filed under. The mirror ships a libm-baseline harness, examples/c/sources/Entropy.c (naive p*log(p) loop with libm log versus yepMath_Log_V64f_V64f plus yepCore_DotProduct on 16M doubles, built with -O3 by examples/c/Makefile), but no published output. Independent reports contradict the 3x on newer machines (WebSearch snippets only, discourse.julialang.org EGRESS_BLOCKED): in the 2019 Julia Discourse thread 'Performance of log.(x)' Yeppp.log was about twice as slow as Base log on one machine, and posters note its speed is inconsistent across architectures, sometimes slower than an unvectorized loop, because the precompiled 2014-2015 binary dispatches on CPU models it recognizes. The official Bitbucket repository (bitbucket.org/MDukhan/yeppp) returns 404, so repo_url is the unofficial GitHub mirror (last commit 2015-08-24 'Build: new build system based on Ninja + Python'; its README is a FAQ with no benchmarks). The project's own comparisons against MKL/libm on yeppp.info and docs.yeppp.info, the PPAM 2013 paper (Dukhan and Vuduc) and the Hot Chips 25 poster were EGRESS_BLOCKED and are not recorded. Abandoned since 2015.

notes: 3x claim and snippet confirmed verbatim in the Yeppp.jl README; tier C stays (claim without methodology, baseline Julia Base log rather than libm). Main shortcomings: off the <cmath> baseline, no hardware or methodology, contradicted by later Julia Discourse reports of Yeppp.log 2x slower than Base on some CPUs (snippet only), abandoned unofficial mirror with the official Bitbucket repo gone.
